Twenty comments

Gan Ainm Waltz, place of origin unknown to me.

This features on an album called “Mr. Universe” , of English melodeon player and singer Tony Hall. It is the first of two waltz tunes on that album in a set he calls “Local Hero”, as the second one is The Mist-Covered Mountains, used in the soundtrack of that film. As I don’t have the CD packet I couldn’t refer to thet for the tune’s name, which might not be on it anyway.

↳ Posted by nicholas on January 25th, 2007.

As played on the album, it wasn’t easy at times to follow the tune, played fairly slowly with a lot of chordal stuff - very nicely, in fact. So even if I did get the main drift of it, which isn’t certain, there are probably parallel lines the melody could follow, at least in places. Oh, and there’s a middle C put in the sheet music an octave too low.

↳ Posted by nicholas on January 25th, 2007.

Bob McQuillen

Amelia’s Waltz was written around 1980 by by Bob McQuillen. He named the tune for Amelia Stiles, Deanna Stiles’ daughter. Amelia was born in a famous packing crate, which carried Lindbergh’s airplane back to the US from Europe. Amelia herself was named after Amelia Earhart. At the time we were all living in the New England woods, making money however we were able and playing music as much as we could. Lindbergh’s crate was beside the Blackwater River and Deanna lived there for years. The crate is now the center of The Lindbergh Crate Museum, in Canaan, Maine.

Bob McQuillen is pretty much the dean of contradance musicians. He received a National Heritage Fellowship Award in September from the National Endowment for the Arts. McQuillen recently celebrated his 50th anniversary playing dances. Over the years he has been a member of Ralph Page’s Orchestra, the Canterbury Orchestra, New England Tradition, and other important bands. In addition, McQuillen has published ten notebooks containing the hundreds of dance tunes that he has written, many of which have become standards in the contradance repertoire.

Bob McQuillen plays now with Old New England, composed of Deanna Stiles on flute and fiddle, Jane Orzechowski on fiddle, and Bob on piano and accordion.

↳ Posted by David Levine on March 13th, 2007.

“Amelia’s Waltz” ~ by Bob McQuillen

I was surprised this wasn’t already here, which again shows I shouldn’t take things for granted. This tune is always fitted to the flute or whistle, so here is a transcript with that in mind, and with a few other possibilities tune-wise. On the intro it can also go ~

Ken Burns’ Mark Twain documentary soundtrack

I was quite pleasantly surprised to have that “Hey, wait, I know this tune!” epiphany roundabout 1:06:30 of part one. Very nice piano rendition. Re: Amelia

Setting number 2, transcribed and contributed around 2007 by David Levin, has an A# in bar 7 of the A part on the sheet music. According to a comment several years later that is incorrect, and David seems to agree.

What would be “correct”, if there is such a thing? Or have the years of that version circulating made it just another setting?

↳ Posted by amo amas on July 13th, 2025.

Re: Amelia

“What would be “correct”, if there is such a thing?”

I’ve always played an A# there, but I’m guessing that, from looking at various online scores, the original might have been a B, as in |D2 B,3 B,|B,4 A,2| for bars 7 and 8. That’s also what’s given in the King Street Sessions tunebook. Some people also play an A.

But, really, surely part of the folk process is allowing variations from the original.

↳ Posted by DonaldK on July 13th, 2025.

Re: Amelia

Yes, it wasn’t A# originally. It was originally published in Note Book #5 by Bob McQuillen. What an amazing guy he must have been!

You can see the original published version at https://cdss.org/elibrary/mcquillen/totm.html#amelia

I was introduced to the tune via a session handout print of setting #2. I wonder if people were playing the A# before that version was posted here.

Amelia, X:5

X:5 is close to the published version from Bob Quinlin’s little book with just a couple of changes: I’ve kept the first ending and chords from X:2 and changed the second to the last measure. The original has a dotted eighth note there, i.e., |d2 dotted-e c2|, which I decided must have been an error.
